projects.title: CAMP v2
projects.short: The board 200 students built at Technocamp: an Arduino Nano CubeSat payload computer, all through-hole.
lead: CAMP v2 is the board I designed for the electronics class at Technocamp 2026. It's an 80 × 80 mm carrier for an Arduino Nano that reads temperature, humidity and carbon monoxide, shows them on a small screen and sends them over USB. That's the same job the payload computer of a real CubeSat does.

Every part is through-hole, so a 12-year-old can solder it with a normal iron and no magnifying glass. The board has no chips of its own. The Nano does the thinking, and the board gives it clean wiring, the right resistors in the right places, and connectors that only fit one way.

cover.alt: Top side of the CAMP v2 PCB
cover.caption: Top side, rev B. The silkscreen says notazizelse@github.

facts: DHT11 temperature + humidity, MQ-7 carbon monoxide
16×2 I²C LCD, two RGB LEDs, three buttons, USB serial
KiCad 10, LCSC parts, JLCPCB production files
Technocamp 2026, Robotics & Engineering Association, Turin Polytechnic University in Tashkent

p: At Technocamp I taught 200 students aged 12 to 17 to design PCBs and etch them with chemicals in a camp in the mountains. They needed a board that does something real, that a beginner can assemble, and that still teaches proper wiring. Loose sensor modules on a breadboard fall apart, so this board turns them into one instrument.

The sensors and buttons on the left tell the Arduino something. The screen and LEDs on the right are how the Arduino tells you something. Nothing talks to anything else directly, every signal goes through the Nano. The LEDs sit in sockets so they can be swapped, and a jumper picks common-cathode or common-anode LEDs.

The build guide, troubleshooting guide and hardware reference are written in English and Uzbek. The back of the board says PER ASPERA AD ASTRA. This autumn I'm using the same board to teach 20 students at Turin Polytechnic, with boards ordered from China this time instead of etched by hand.

projects.title: Glasses for dyslexic readers
projects.short: Press a button on the glasses and they photograph the page and read it out loud.
lead: Glasses with a button. Press it and a camera on the frame photographs the printed page in front of you, sends it to my server, and a reading screen reads it out loud with word-by-word highlighting. The reading screen also lets you change letter spacing, word spacing, size and font (Lexend, Atkinson Hyperlegible or OpenDyslexic), which is what actually helps a lot of dyslexic readers.
The glasses only take the photo. The server cleans it up with OpenCV and reads it with Tesseract in English, Russian and Uzbek. Parts cost about 190,000 sum.
facts: LiPo, TP4056 charger, MT3608 boost to 5 V
3D printed in PETG, designed in Fusion 360

list: Press the button. The ESP32-CAM on the frame takes a photo with the flash on.
It sends the photo over HTTPS, through a phone hotspot, to my server.
The server straightens and cleans the image with OpenCV and reads it with Tesseract.
The reading screen, on any phone or laptop, shows the text with your spacing and font, and reads it out loud word by word, into Bluetooth earbuds if you want.

p: If the venue has no mobile data, a laptop runs the same server and the glasses switch to it. If the glasses fail on stage, the reading screen has a Take photo button that sends a phone photo through the same path.

The server is live and has read its first test photo. The frame and the pitch are being finished for demo day on Friday, 9 October 2026. The code is in a private repo for now because it has deploy details for the server in it.

projects.title: Haven Tashkent
projects.short: A free two-day game jam for teenagers in Tashkent that I'm organising.
lead: Hack Club Haven is about 200 game jams in about 200 cities, all run by high schoolers on the same weekend. Teenagers aged 13 to 18 get two days to build a game and publish it on itch.io with the code on GitHub. It's free.
I'm the lead organiser of the Tashkent one, on 14–15 November 2026. We're a team of 14.

cover.alt: Haven Tashkent banner with the Tashkent skyline and a hedgehog in a doppi
cover.caption: Our banner

facts: About 180 signups and 100 people in the room

p: I run the team, the venue search, sponsors and workshops. So far that's 85 personalised sponsor emails, a proposal kit for 70 sponsors in Uzbek, Russian and English, and three sponsors on board. Every organiser also had to ship their own small game first. Mine is [Jumpio](slug:jumpio).

list: [Haven Hub](slug:haven-hub), the team hub we run the whole event on. It's live at [haventash.xyz](https://haventash.xyz).
A [Telegram registration bot](slug:haven-bot) in three languages, with referrals and a leaderboard.
Die-cut [PCB name badges](slug:badges), made by PCBWay.
The posters, flyers and profile pictures below, drawn by my own Python scripts instead of an image generator.

projects.title: Haven Hub
projects.short: Team hub for Hack Club Haven organisers. Runs haventash.xyz.
lead: A free team hub for Hack Club Haven organisers in any city. Every organiser gets their own task list with proof and reminders over Telegram or email, the leads get a dashboard, and the event gets a public page and an Apply page in English, Uzbek and Russian.
It runs on a Google Sheet you own, or on its own small server, which is how [haventash.xyz](https://haventash.xyz) runs. I shipped versions 4.0 to 5.1 in five days, because our team needed it.

cover.caption: The lead's overview: what's overdue, what's blocked, signups and money from HQ. (Made-up team.)

facts: Plain ES modules, no build step, no framework
One Google Apps Script file, or Node 22 + SQLite

p: Organising Haven means 14 people and a lot of tasks with deadlines. So each person sees only their own tasks with the steps, the deadline and who to ask, presses Start, Done (with proof) or I'm blocked, and gets a reminder the evening before. The leads see everything.
The demo runs the real back end in your browser against a fake Google Sheet with a made-up team, so you can click everything and nothing gets sent anywhere.

projects.title: Haven PCB badges
projects.short: Die-cut name badges for Haven that are also circuit boards. Art generated in Python, made by PCBWay.
lead: Name badges for Haven Tashkent, made as PCBs: lime-green HACKER for participants and brown ORGANIZER for the team. They're die-cut to the shape of the art, 55.9 × 59.1 mm, with a gold (ENIG) finish and a full-colour print on the front. PCBWay is sponsoring the manufacturing.

p: One Python generator draws every layer from a single file of numbers: the board outline, the copper and mask art that gets imported into KiCad, the colour-print files PCBWay needs, and these mock-ups. If the outline changes by a millimetre, I change one number and regenerate everything instead of redrawing it.

projects.title: Orbita CanSat & IREC
projects.short: My season as lead electronics engineer for the national CanSat and rocketry teams.
lead: I was selected as lead electronics engineer for Uzbekistan's national team at the International Space Tournament "Orbita", where teams build a 3U CubeSat around a supplied kit, add their own payload, and fly it to the stratosphere on a balloon. I'm also on our IREC rocketry team, working on thrust control.
Our Orbita team won internationally last year, before I joined. That one is theirs. I'm the new lead.
facts: 3U CubeSat, flown on a stratospheric balloon

p: The season has just started. Before drawing anything I wrote research: a playbook on how Orbita works, a technician's study of possible missions, and a study on using the camera as a real instrument instead of a photo taker. Together they go through dozens of mission ideas, what's actually new, and how each would be built. They're below in full. The flight PCB is what I'm drawing now.

projects.title: WIT stratospheric payload
projects.short: A 3U balloon payload planned down to the byte: 7 missions, a 4-layer STM32F407 board, dual LoRa.
lead: The design package for a 3U stratospheric balloon payload, for a Women in Tech Uzbekistan project. Seven science missions, one 4-layer board with an STM32F407, two LoRa radios, a Geiger counter, a power budget, a test plan and a 91-byte telemetry packet.
All of it was planned before opening KiCad. Every part has a written reason, and so does every part that wasn't picked.

projects.title: KarateFC
projects.short: A Betaflight flight controller for drones that are supposed to crash.
lead: My next flight controller, in the class of the SpeedyBee F405 V3: STM32F405, USB-C, Betaflight-compatible. It's for fast research drones that get destroyed on purpose at the end of each test.

That changes the whole design. Normal FPV boards are built to survive a crash and get repaired. Here the board dies anyway, so what matters is cost per unit, how fast I can build a batch, and that it stays reliable right up until impact.

p: A separate 4-in-1 ESC stack, or the ESCs on the flight controller (AIO)? For drones that get thrown away, fewer boards and fewer connectors usually wins. At Unique Dynamic I wrote a flight controller's firmware from zero. This time I'm using Betaflight so the effort goes into the hardware.

projects.title: Vocabio
projects.short: The SAT vocabulary app I made from my own Anki deck. Works offline.
lead: I was studying the College Panda's 400 SAT words in Anki and wanted something that could also read the words to me. So I took my Anki export, kept all my progress (1,424 reviews), rewrote all 400 definitions to be shorter (42% on average) and gave every word an example sentence and synonyms.
It has an Anki-style review mode and a hands-free listen mode. It works offline, installs on an iPhone from Safari, and there's a Windows app. Progress syncs between them.

projects.title: Kitchen Queue
projects.short: A camera counts the canteen line so students know when to go.
lead: Our canteen line is long at lunch and nobody knows whether to go now or in ten minutes. Kitchen Queue uses a camera that's already there, counts the people in line with computer vision, and shows a live count, a wait estimate and a "typical for this weekday" chart that tells you whether waiting helps.

Only one number leaves the building every 10 seconds. The live picture is optional and stays behind an access code. The demo uses made-up numbers. The real version is meant for the school's cameras, so its code is private.

cover.alt: Kitchen Queue demo showing 27 people in line and a chart of the school day
cover.caption: The demo at the lunch bell

facts: YOLO, MobileNet-SSD or HOG with OpenCV, on whatever PC sees the camera
Python standard library, live updates over Server-Sent Events
An ESP32 uplink sketch for places without a PC

p: A small counter script reads the camera stream, counts people in the queue area and posts a number to the server. Everything only dials out, so the school network needs no changes and nothing is exposed. The server keeps 28 days of counts, which is what makes the weekday forecast work.

projects.title: Anki Listen Mode
projects.short: Anki add-on that reads your cards out loud and moves on by itself.
lead: The open-source spin-off of [Vocabio](slug:vocabio)'s listen mode, as an Anki add-on. It reads each card aloud with Anki's built-in text-to-speech and moves on by itself, and it never writes to your collection.

projects.title: STM32 Homebrew fix
projects.short: Fixes the two usual build failures with Homebrew's ARM GCC on macOS.
lead: If you build CubeMX projects in VS Code on a Mac with Homebrew's arm-none-eabi-gcc, two things usually break: the toolchain has no newlib, and the Makefile points at a gcc without a sysroot. This script fixes both.
